# Question 1

### a

Covariates are "supplementary variables that predict outcomes" (G & G
95). They are not required for unbiased estimation. They're used to
improve precision by reducing variance in potential outcomes or
differences between treatment and control observations in OLS, and to
assign blocks in block randomized assignment. In theory, they are
measured before subjects are randomized into treatment and control.

### b

"Disturbance term" refers to the part of a regression that is
unobserved, which is unexplained variation in untreated and treated
outcomes.

### c

Equation 4.2 demonstrates that rescaling the outcome by subtracting a
pretest leads to unbiased estimates of the ATE. Subtracting the rescaled
pretest $cX_j$ instead of the pre-test $X_i$ would....(show it produces
unbaised estiamtes of the ATE).

Equation 4.2 says

$$
E(\hat{ATE}) = E[Y_i - X_i|D_i = 1] - E[Y_i-X_i|D_i = 0]
$$

The rescaled pretest $cX_i$ where $c$ is constant and positive can be
substituted for $X_i$.

$$
E(\hat{ATE}) = E[Y_i - cX_i|D_i = 1] - E[Y_i-cX_i|D_i = 0]
$$

So when we expand as in 4.2:

$$
E(\hat{ATE}) = E[Y_i|D_i = 1] - E[cX_i|D_i=1] - E[Y_i|D_i = 0] + cE[X_i|Di=0]
$$

...and rearrange:

$$
E(\hat{ATE}) = E[Y_i|D_i = 1] - E[Y_i|D_i = 0] - c(E[X_i|D_i=1]  + E[X_i|Di=0])
$$

...and because we assume that the expected values of $Y_i$ when
$D_i = 0$ are the same as when $D_i = 1$, we arrive at the same place as
in figure 4.2:

$$
 E(\hat{ATE}) = E(Y_i(1))-E[Y_i(0)]
$$

### d

The slope parameter $b$ in equation 4.7 is the change in average
potential outcomes $\mu_{Y1} - \mu_{Y0}$, also called the ATE.

$$
E(ATE) = E[Y_i(1)] - E[Y_i(0)]
$$

### e

Balanced designs are ideal because they allow for interval estimation:
CI's will be conservative rather than too wide or narrow from outcome
variances with imbalance in the treatment and controls that produce.
They're particularly helpful when there is similar variance in the
outcomes of treatment and control groups.

## Question 2

### a.

RI to test the null that pre-test scores are unaffected by treatment
assignment.

```{r}
data_2 <- read.csv("/Users/kom11/Documents/GitHub/regression-study/Experiments/doi-10.60600-yu-vuh8kd/Gendelman_2004.csv")

set.seed(312608170)

names(data_2)

subject <- data_2$subject
treatment <- data_2$treatment
pretest <- data_2$pretest
posttest <- data_2$posttest
improvement <- data_2$improvement

model_2 <- lm_robust(treatment ~ pretest)

fstat_2 <- model_2$fstatistic[1] # get the f stat of treatment

fstat_2

# now random. inference with f-stat to get a p-value:

ra_2 <- declare_ra(nrow(data_2), m = 9) # random assignment procedure

perm_matrx_2 <- obtain_permutation_matrix(ra_2) #10k randomization permmatrix

estimates_2 <- c() #bucket to store results

for (i in 1:ncol(perm_matrx_2)) {
  
  data_2$ri <- perm_matrx_2[, i]
  
  random_inf_2 <- lm_robust(data_2$ri ~ data_2$pretest)
  
  estimates_2 <- c(estimates_2, random_inf_2$fstatistic[1])
  
}

```

The reported p-value is:

```{r}
print(mean(estimates_2 >= random_inf_2$fstatistic))
```

We can't reject the null hypothesis that treatment had no effect on
pretest scores because 0.2093 is much higher than 0.05. In this case,
rejecting the null means randomization was successful.

Now 95% CI constructed with randomization inference:

```{r}

set.seed(312608170)

null <- 0

dim_estimates_2 <- c()

data_2 <- data_2 %>%
  mutate(
    y0_null = case_when(
      treatment == 0 ~ posttest,
      treatment == 1 ~ posttest - null
    ),
    y1_null = case_when(
      treatment == 1 ~ posttest,
      treatment == 0 ~ posttest + null
    )
  )

unique(data_2$y1_null - data_2$y0_null == null)

```

```{r}

for(i in 1:ncol(perm_matrx_2)){
 
   data_2$ri <- perm_matrx_2[, i] #hypothetical assignment
  
  
  data_2$y_temp <- ifelse(
    data_2$ri == 1,
    data_2$y1_null,
    data_2$y0_null
  )
  
  mean_treated <- mean(data_2$y_temp[data_2$ri == 1]) #DIM
  mean_control <- mean(data_2$y_temp[data_2$ri == 0])
  
  dim_estimates_2[i] <- mean_treated - mean_control #store 
  
}

mean(dim_estimates_2) # should be centered around 0

# CI?

ci_2

```

The interval is wider than for the DIM estimation of the effect of

## Question 3

This reporting policy does not offer up unbiased estimates because it is
premised on the outcomes -- seems like rather explicit
researcher-induced bias. Whether or not to report results based on
covariates included should only be decided by theory and expectations
(pre-registered, ideally, hypotheses).

### Question 5


```{r, echo = T, include = T, warning = F}
data_5 <- read.csv("./doi-10.60600-yu-vuh8kd/GerberGreenBook_Chapter4_Table_4_1.csv")
```


#### a

```{r, echo = T, include = T, warning = F}
# restriction that a regression of $d_i$ on $X_i$ (the pre-test) generates and F stat whose reported p value is greater that 0.05. Ie were assigned $d_i$  significantly predicted by $X-i$, RI would be conducted again until $d_i$ met criterion.

# d is dataset, z is generated treatment assignment vector, x is name of covariate, m = number of schools assigned to treatment
restricted_assignment_5 <- function (d, x, m) {
  while (TRUE) {
   
    Z <- complete_ra(nrow(d), m) #generate a complete RA
    
    d$Z <- Z # add assignment to temporary df
    
    fit <- lm_robust(as.formula(paste("Z ~", x)),
                     data = d)
    
    f <- fit$fstatistic #has 3 numbers: value of F stat, numerator DoF, Denom DoF
    
    p.val <- 1 - pf(q = f[1], df1 = f[2], df2 = f[3])
    
    # keep only restriction-satisfier assignments
    if (p.val > 0.05){
      return(Z)
    }
  }
}

set.seed(6081709)

#  randomization (restricted) iterations
sim_matrix_5 <- replicate(10000, 
                           restricted_assignment_5(d = data_5, x = "x", 
                                         m = sum(data_5$D)))

# f stat where reported p val greater than 0.05?

fp <- c()

for (i in 1:ncol(sim_matrix_5)) {
  data_5$d_temp = sim_matrix_5[, i]
  f <- lm_robust(d_temp ~ x, data_5)$fstatistic
  fp[i] <- 1 - pf(q = f[1], df1 = f[2], df2 = f[3])
}

min(fp)

all(fp > 0.05)

```

The min value of the created vector a p vals is just above the
threshhold in a generous read (0.05005606 -\> 0.05006 \> 0.05000). I'm
not sure if the hypothetical researcher would but I'll take this as
sufficient to proceed.

Weights?
```{r, echo = T, include = T, warning = F}

# about inverse probability weights

# already made matrix of treatment assignments to calculate the probabilities (matrix_5)

# can I use obtain conditional probabilities? 

declare_5 <- declare_ra(permutation_matrix = sim_matrix_5)
declare_5 #declared restricted assignment  procedure

# calculate probabilities and IPWs
data_5 <- data_5 %>%
  mutate(
    probs = obtain_condition_probabilities(declare_5, D),
    weights = 1 / probs
  )

# compare weights for treated units and control
data_5 %>%
  group_by(D) %>%
  summarize(
    mean_weight = mean(weights),
    sd_w = sd(weights),
    min_w = min(weights),
    max_w = max(weights),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

```

Weights vary by 0.024 SDs in the control group and by 0.018 in the
treatment group.That seems like a small difference (ie, observed variation in estimated weights is small), and otherwise they are comperable. I know we can't always assume that balance in terms of numbers in treatment and control has anything to do with covariate balance (or, equal C/T group size alone doesn't mean equal probability of being treated).Here also reversing treatment or control assignment does not change the F stat (with 20 of 40 schools treated, true probability of being treated is 0.5, so everyone's weight is 2).

#### b

```{r, echo = T, include = T, warning = F}

# constructing observed outcomes

#  actual DIM, weighted

data_5$obs_y <- ifelse(data_5$D == 1, 
                       data_5$y1, 
                       data_5$y0)

#estimate original treatment-control difference with 5a IPW
dim_5 <- difference_in_means(obs_y ~ D, weights = weights, data = data_5)

ate_dim_5 <- coef(dim_5)["D"] #treatment coefficient

print(ate_dim_5)

# sampling distribution under the null Y1 = Y0


#probability assigned to treatment x restricted randomizations:
p_treat_5 <- rowMeans(sim_matrix_5)

set.seed(6081709)

dim_estimates_5 <- rep(NA, ncol(sim_matrix_5))

## RI 
for (i in 1:ncol(sim_matrix_5)) {
  
  data_5$ri <- sim_matrix_5[, i] # sim treatment assignment
  
  
  data_5$w_ri <- ifelse( #IPW re: simulated assignment
    data_5$ri == 1, 
    1 / p_treat_5,
    1 / (1 - p_treat_5) 
  )
  
# est treatment effect under sharp null
    dim_estimates_5 [i] <- coef(
      lm_robust(obs_y ~ ri, weights = w_ri, data = data_5)
      )["ri"]
}

print(mean(dim_estimates_5)) # is center on 0

print(mean(abs(dim_estimates_5) >= abs(ate_dim_5))) # p-value 

```

The p-value of 0.0046 lets us reject the sharp null: observed treatment effect is unusual enough under the sharp null (Y1=Y0) to reject the hypothesis of no treatment effect. 

#### c

```{r, echo = T, include = T, warning = F}

# actual coefficients (weighted, covariate-adjusted)

model_5c <- lm_robust(obs_y ~ D + x, 
                                      weights = weights, #ip each schools original assignment
                                      data = data_5)

summary(model_5c)

coef_5c <- coef(model_5c)["D"]

print(coef_5c)

# do RI
 # have sim_matrix_5: 10k criteria-meeting assignments ; obs_y: original observed post scores that under sharp null should be same for unit if treated as if untreated; p_treat_5: probability assigned to treatment x restricted randomizations

set.seed(6081709)

coef_estimates_5c <- rep(NA, 10000)

# estimating covariate-adjusted regression 

for (i in 1:ncol(sim_matrix_5)) {
  
  data_5$ri <- sim_matrix_5[, i]
  
   data_5$w_ri <- ifelse( #IPW re: simulated assignment
    data_5$ri == 1, 
    1 / p_treat_5,
    1 / (1 - p_treat_5) 
  )

   # est treatment effect under sharp null
    coef_estimates_5c [i] <- coef(
      lm_robust(obs_y ~ ri + x, weights = w_ri, data = data_5)
      )["ri"]
  

}


# checking that the distribution is centred around 0

print(mean(coef_estimates_5c))

# calculating the p-value 

print(mean(abs(coef_estimates_5c) >= abs(coef_5c))) 

# compare sampling variability without then with cov adjustment 
sd(dim_estimates_5)

sd(coef_estimates_5c)
```

Here we get a two-sided p-val of 0.0029 which is less than 0.05 (we would very infrequently generate a covariate-adjusted treatment coefficient at least as extreme as that observed if treatment had no effect) we can
reject the sharp null (no effect for any school).

Sampling variability shrinks notably with covariate adjustment -- it "worked."


```{r}

ggplot(
  df_5d,
  aes(x = value, color = assignment)
) +
  geom_density(linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~estimator) +
  labs(
    title = "Sampling Distributions Under Sharp Null",
    x = "Estimated treatment effect",
    y = "Density",
    color = "Assignment Procedure"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

```
The standard deviations reflect variability in estimated treatment effects across hypothetical random assignments. We see restricted randomization did reduce the SD, so "worked" in the sense that some variation the covariate would have 'controlled' was eliminated, by excluding hypothetical random assignments that would have had more of a relationship between covariates and the outcome (reduces chance covariate imbalance to sampling variability). The exclusion restriction of 0.05 might be a bit lax and only reduce extreme cases.

Comparing restricted randomization having adjustd for covariates: the difference is fairly negligible (see lefthand side of the plot above). This makes sense: regression already adjusts for pre-treatment scores, reducing whatever differences those scores would be associated with vis-a-vis estimates of treatment effects. 

Perhaps the topline is restricted randomization and regression adjustment are able to address the same (or some of the same) conduits for sampling variability. At the same time, one (at least RR) doesn't eliminate the value of the other (CA).

```{r, echo = T, include = T, warning = F}

f_observed_6

# now ri

  repeated_f_tests[i] <- lm_robust(

}


# r i p value
mean(repeated_f_tests >= f_observed_6)
```

This distribution of p-values indicates that the groups are not

```{r, echo = T, include = T, warning = F}

data_7 <- data.frame(

delcaration_7

# running a for loop to assess sampling variance of DIM estimator
# I use the standard R var function as we have no reason

# creating empty vector to store results of for loop

dim_estimates_7 <- numeric(ncol(D_7))

# estimating dim 

for (i in 1:ncol(D_7)) {
  
  data_7$ri <- D_7[, i]
  
  treated_mean <- mean(data_7$Y1[data_7$ri == 1])

  dim_estimates_7[i] <- treated_mean - control_mean

  (dim_estimates_7 - mean(dim_estimates_7))^2
   )

var_7a
```

Sampling Variance is 2.833

#### b

```{r, echo = T, include = T, warning = F}

# run randomizations separately for each blocking scheme,  then cbind

# creating block assignments

block_options <- list(
  list(c("A","B"), c("C","D")),
  list(c("A","C"), c("B","D")),
  list(c("A","D"), c("B","C"))
)

get_block_data <- function(block_options, data) {
  
  subjects_ordered <- unlist(block_options)
  
  block_data <- data[match(subjects_ordered, data$Subject), ]
  
  block_data$Block <- rep(1:length(block_options), each = 2)
  
  return(block_data)
}

block_datasets <- lapply(block_options, get_block_data, data = data_7)

names(block_datasets) <- paste0("BlockOption", 1:3)

BlockOption1 <- block_datasets$BlockOption1
BlockOption2 <- block_datasets$BlockOption2
BlockOption3 <- block_datasets$BlockOption3

# randomising within blocking options - 1

delcaration_71 <- declare_ra(
  N = nrow(BlockOption1), 
  blocks = BlockOption1$Block,
  block_m = rep(1, length(unique(BlockOption1$Block))) 
)
delcaration_71

# randomising within blocking options - 2

delcaration_72 <- declare_ra(
  N = nrow(BlockOption2), 
  blocks = BlockOption2$Block,
  block_m = rep(1, length(unique(BlockOption2$Block))) 
)
delcaration_72

# randomising within blocking options - 3

delcaration_73 <- declare_ra(
  N = nrow(BlockOption3), 
  blocks = BlockOption3$Block,
  block_m = rep(1, length(unique(BlockOption3$Block))) 
)
delcaration_73

library(randomizr)

# extracting assignment vectors for each blocking optioon - 1 -3

assignment1 <- obtain_permutation_matrix(delcaration_71)
assignment2 <- obtain_permutation_matrix(delcaration_72)
assignment3 <- obtain_permutation_matrix(delcaration_73)

# reorder matrix rows so they match data_7 order


assignment1 <- assignment1[
  match(data_7$Subject, BlockOption1$Subject),
  , drop = FALSE
]

assignment2 <- assignment2[
  match(data_7$Subject, BlockOption2$Subject),
  , drop = FALSE
]

assignment3 <- assignment3[
  match(data_7$Subject, BlockOption3$Subject),
  , drop = FALSE
]

# combining for permmatrix of unique random assignments

perm_matrix_7b <- cbind(assignment1, assignment2, assignment3)


dim(perm_matrix_7b)

# running a for loop to assess sampling variance of DIM estimator
# I use the standard R var function as we have no reason 
# to believe this is the population

# setting seed

set.seed(6081709)

# creating empty vector to store results of for loop

dim_estimates_7b <- numeric(ncol(perm_matrix_7b))

# estimating dim 

for (i in 1:ncol(perm_matrix_7b)) {
  data_7$ri <- perm_matrix_7b[, i]
  
  treated_mean <- mean(data_7$Y1[data_7$ri == 1])
  control_mean <- mean(data_7$Y0[data_7$ri == 0])
  
  
  dim_estimates_7b[i] <- treated_mean - control_mean
}

  #sampling variance
  var_7b <- mean(
  (dim_estimates_7b - mean(dim_estimates_7b))^2
   )


var_7b

```

Variance is 2.833, same as in 7a. 

### c

Randomly bocking or blocking on a non-prognostic covariate does not increase precision by design. It could by accident I suppose (or would that mean blocking on a covariate that is in fact progrostic, though not known to be?) but we see here that it can instead produce identical sampling variance as that given by complete random assignment.

## d

The OLS weights consider within-block balance and the size of blocks for

## e

```{r}
# assignment counts per block
table(data_9$strata, data_9$treat2)

# get assignment probabilities and IPWs

data_9_weighted <- data_9 %>%
  group_by(strata) %>%
  mutate(

    p_treat = mean(treat2 == 1),# proport assigned to treatment in each block

    q = ifelse( # p(receiving observed condition)
      treat2 == 1,
      p_treat,
      1 - p_treat
    ),

    weight = 1 / q #ipw

  ) %>%
  ungroup()


#regress after inverting weights

model_9e <- lm_robust(
  vote02 ~ treat2,
  weights = weight,
  data = data_9_weighted
)

summary(model_9e)
# would then regress weighted vote on treatment

ate_9e <- coef(model_9e)["treat2"]

ate_9e


model_9e_blocks <- lm_robust(
  vote02 ~ treat2 + as.factor(strata),
  weights = weight,
  data = data_9_weighted
)

coef(model_9e_blocks)["treat2"]
```
Reproduced reported -0.00783 for weighted regression with blocking included, and weighted regression without blocking.

```{r}

vote_vars_10

  response = "treatment"

f_stat_10
```

```{r}

# RI to test null that none of those vars preidcts treatment
# means cluster assignment

clusters_10 <- data_10 %>% #28 row summary for counting treated precincts
  group_by(unit) %>%
  summarize(
    treated = mean(treatment)
  )

declaration_10 = declare_ra(
  N = nrow(data_10),
  clusters = data_10$unit, #IDs precinct for each voter
  m = sum(clusters_10$treated))

declaration_10

```

```{r}
set.seed(6081709)

# RI

estimates_10 <- numeric(10000)

# f stats


for(i in 1:10000) {
  
  data_10$ri <- conduct_ra(declaration_10) #precint level assignment
  
  
  avoiding_long_type_2 <- reformulate(vote_vars_10,
                                    response = "ri")
  
  m10_temp <- lm_robust(avoiding_long_type_2, data = data_10) #get F stat for given assignment
  
  
estimates_10 [i] <- summary(m10_temp)$fstatistic[1]

}

pval10 <- mean((estimates_10) >= abs(f_stat_10)) #RI p val

f_stat_10
pval10

```
We cannot reject the null: observed association between turnout and treatment assignment is not distinguishable from (or not unusually large compared to) that which randomization by precinct could have produced by chance (ie not evidence of problematic covariate imbalance). 93.7% of simulated cluster assignments produced F-stats at least as large as 1.654.


### b
Have: declaration_10, clusters_10, vote_vars_10 is list of past votes
```{r}

prep_10b <- reformulate(
  c("treatment", vote_vars_10), #list of past votes
  response = "vote03"
)

model_10b <- lm_robust(
  prep_10b,
  data = data_10,
  clusters = unit #calc SEs acct for w/in precint dependence
)

summary(model_10b)

ate_10b <- model_10b$coefficients["treatment"]

ate_10b


```
Assignment to a treated precinct is associated with an increase of 5.6 percentage poings in one's probability of voting in 2003, net of voting across the other 20 elections. The adjusted R2 suggests that 32.23% of observed variation in 2003 turnout (individual) is explained by the model containing turnout in past elections and treatment assignment.

```{r}

# RI to test sharp null treated outcome = untreated outcome



avoiding_long_type_2 <- reformulate(
    c("ri", vote_vars_10), #replace treatment with RI
    response = "vote03"
    )

# RI
set.seed(6081709)

n_sims_10b <- 10000

estimates_10b <- numeric(n_sims_10b)


# sim cluster assignments, est coefs

for(i in 1:10000) {
  
  data_10$ri <- conduct_ra(declaration_10) #precint level assignment
  

  m10_temp <- lm_robust(avoiding_long_type_2, data = data_10) 
  
  estimates_10b[i] <- coef(m10_temp)["ri"] #get coef on simulated treatment assignment

}

# p val

pval10b <- mean(
  abs(estimates_10b) >= abs(ate_10b)
)

pval10b

```

Sharp null: Y0 = Y1. The p value for this sharp null is 0.0045 -- this is less than the standard 0.05 cutoff and 0.01. Thus we can  reject the null hypothesis (at both the 5% and 1% significance levels) that experimental assignment had no effect on decisions to vote in 2003 (only 0.45% of simulated random assignments under the sharp null generated treatment effects as extreme as that reported in the observed ATE.
